stem: A teammate adds `src/analytics.d.ts` to a project. What can a `.d.ts` file contain, and what does the compiler emit for it?

options.text: Any TypeScript code; the compiler emits a matching `.js` file next to it at build time
options.why: Declaration files may not contain implementations, and nothing is emitted for them.

options.text: Types and `declare` forms only, with no implementations; it emits no JavaScript
options.why: A .d.ts describes code that exists somewhere else, so it compiles to nothing.

options.text: Only interfaces and type aliases; `declare const` and `declare function` are reserved for `.ts` files
options.why: Ambient value declarations such as `declare const` and `declare function` are exactly what .d.ts files are for.

options.text: Runtime polyfills that TypeScript injects into the bundle before the rest of your code runs
options.why: TypeScript never injects code from declaration files; they are erased completely.

explanation: A declaration file is a type-only description of JavaScript that exists elsewhere: in a library, a global script or the runtime. It can hold interfaces, type aliases and `declare` forms (`declare const`, `declare function`, `declare class`, `declare module`, `declare global`), but no function bodies or initializers. The compiler reads it for checking and emits nothing for it.

options.text: True
options.why: `declare` only tells the checker that the value exists; the declaration itself is erased from the output.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the emit is just `export const url = API_URL + "/v1";`, so something else must define API_URL at runtime.

explanation: An ambient declaration creates no runtime value. tsc emits `export const url = API_URL + "/v1";` and trusts that `API_URL` is provided by a bundler define, a script tag or the host. If nothing provides it, the code throws a ReferenceError at runtime even though it type-checks.

stem: `import slugify from "legacy-slugify";` fails under `strict` with error TS7016: "Could not find a declaration file for module 'legacy-slugify'. '…/index.js' implicitly has an 'any' type." What is the best first thing to try?

options.text: Turn off `strict` for the whole project so that untyped imports are allowed again
options.why: That silences the error by disabling noImplicitAny everywhere, losing type safety across the codebase.

options.text: Rename the import to `require("legacy-slugify")` so that TypeScript stops resolving the package
options.why: A plain require call returns any and skips checking, which hides the problem rather than adding types.

options.text: Look for community typings first: `npm i -D @types/legacy-slugify`
options.why: If DefinitelyTyped has typings, installing them gives full types with no code of your own to maintain.

options.text: Add `// @ts-ignore` above the import line and leave the module typed as an implicit any
options.why: Ignoring the line keeps every use of the module untyped and hides any later errors on that line.

explanation: TS7016 means the package resolved to plain JavaScript with no typings. First look for `@types/<name>` on DefinitelyTyped or a newer version of the package that bundles types. If none exists, write a declaration yourself: either a full `declare module "legacy-slugify" { … }` or, as a stopgap, the shorthand `declare module "legacy-slugify";`.
reference: TypeScript docs: Consumption of declaration files

stem: To silence TS7016 quickly, you add a one-line shorthand ambient module declaration to a `.d.ts` file. Fill in the missing keyword: `____ module "legacy-lib";`
explanation: `declare module "legacy-lib";` is a shorthand ambient module: every import from it is typed `any`. It unblocks the build but gives no checking, so replace it with a real declaration (or @types) when you can.

stem: A Vite project imports images with `import logo from "./logo.svg";`. Which declaration makes this type-check, with `logo` typed as a URL string?

options.text: `declare module "*.svg" { const src: string; export default src; }`
options.why: A wildcard module declaration matches every specifier ending in .svg and describes its default export.

options.text: `declare const logo: string;` at the top of the component that does the importing
options.why: That declares a global variable; the import still fails because no module "./logo.svg" is known.

options.text: `"allowArbitraryExtensions": true` alone, so TypeScript reads the SVG markup as a module
options.why: That flag only lets TS look for a `logo.d.svg.ts` declaration file; it never parses the SVG itself.

options.text: `import logo = require("./logo.svg")`, which skips type checking for non-TS assets
options.why: import-require still needs the module to resolve to declarations, so it fails the same way.

explanation: Bundlers turn asset imports into values (often a URL string), but TypeScript has no idea what `./logo.svg` exports. A wildcard declaration such as `declare module "*.svg"` covers every matching specifier. Frameworks like Vite ship these in `vite/client` types for you.

stem: Match each declaration form with what it describes.

options.text: Adds names to the global scope from inside a module file
options.why: declare global

options.text: Describes, or augments, a module by its import specifier
options.why: declare module

options.text: Describes an existing object that groups values and types, such as a library global
options.why: declare namespace

options.text: Describes a single value that exists at runtime but is defined elsewhere
options.why: declare const

prompts.text: `declare namespace Stripe { function setKey(k: string): void }`

explanation: All four forms are ambient: they describe things that exist at runtime without emitting code. `declare global` only works inside a module file; `declare module "x"` is an augmentation inside a module file and an ambient module declaration inside a script file; `declare namespace` models an object such as a UMD global; `declare const` models one value.

stem: The package `chartkit` ships its own `index.d.ts` (listed in its package.json `"types"`), and a teammate also installed `@types/chartkit`. Which typings does `import { render } from "chartkit"` use?

options.text: `@types/chartkit`, because DefinitelyTyped packages always take priority over bundled types
options.why: TypeScript checks the package itself first and only falls back to @types when it finds no declarations.

options.text: The `index.d.ts` bundled with `chartkit`, because a package's own declarations are found first
options.why: The @types copy is ignored for this import, so it is usually safe to uninstall it.

options.text: Both are merged into one module type, and conflicting members cause duplicate-identifier errors
options.why: Two separate module declaration files for the same specifier are not merged; one resolution wins.

options.text: Neither: the compiler reports an ambiguity error until one of the two packages is removed
options.why: There is no ambiguity error; module resolution simply stops at the first declarations it finds.

explanation: Module resolution looks inside `node_modules/chartkit` first (its `types`/`exports` entries, then a `.d.ts` next to the entry file), and only if that fails does it try `node_modules/@types/chartkit`. Stale @types for a package that now bundles its own types are dead weight and can confuse readers, so remove them.

stem: `import type { User } from "./types";` is removed entirely from the emitted JavaScript, so `./types` is not loaded at runtime because of this line.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: a type-only import is always erased, even under verbatimModuleSyntax.

options.text: False
options.why: Unlike a regular import, `import type` never survives emit, so it cannot trigger the module's side effects.

explanation: `import type` exists precisely so you can depend on a module's types without creating a runtime dependency. It is always erased. That also means you can't use `User` as a value in that file, for example in `instanceof` or as a constructor.
reference: TypeScript 3.8 release notes: Type-only imports and exports

stem: Two files in the same global scope both declare `interface Settings`, one with `theme: string` and one with `fontSize: number`. What is the type of `Settings`?

options.text: Whichever declaration the compiler reads last, which silently replaces the earlier one
options.why: Interfaces never replace each other; same-named interfaces in one scope are combined.

options.text: A compile error, because an interface name can be declared only once in any given scope
options.why: Duplicate interface names are allowed and are the basis of declaration merging.

options.text: One merged interface that requires both `theme: string` and `fontSize: number`
options.why: Declaration merging combines the members of every same-named interface in a scope.

options.text: A union of the two shapes, so a value only needs to match one of the declarations
options.why: Merging adds members together; it does not create a union of alternatives.

explanation: Interfaces are open: same-named interface declarations in one scope merge into a single interface with all members. This is what lets libraries and your own code extend types such as `Window`. Type aliases (`type Settings = …`) are closed; declaring one twice is a duplicate identifier error.

stem: A file with any one of these top-level statements is treated as a module rather than a global script. Which three? (Choose three.)

options.text: `import type { Foo } from "./foo";`
options.why: Any top-level import, even a type-only one, makes the file a module.

options.text: `export const VERSION = "1.0";`
options.why: Any top-level export makes the file a module.

options.text: `export {};`
options.why: An empty export is the idiomatic way to turn a file into a module without exporting anything.

options.text: `/// <reference types="node" />`
options.why: Triple-slash directives are comments that add files to the program; they do not change the file kind.

options.text: `declare namespace Analytics { function track(e: string): void }`
options.why: Ambient namespaces are fine in scripts; they declare globals there.

options.text: `interface Window { appVersion: string }`
options.why: A bare interface is a global declaration in a script; it does not make the file a module.

explanation: TypeScript decides per file: if it has a top-level `import` or `export`, it is a module with its own scope; otherwise it is a script whose declarations are global. This distinction is behind the classic "my global declaration stopped working" bug, where adding an import silently turns global declarations into module-local ones.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Modules (How JavaScript modules are defined)

stem: What does the triple-slash directive `/// <reference types="node" />` at the top of a file do?

options.text: It imports Node's `node:` built-in modules into the file at runtime, like a side-effect import
options.why: Triple-slash directives are compile-time only and emit nothing at runtime.

options.text: It adds `@types/node`, including globals like `process`, to the compilation
options.why: It is a type-only dependency on a types package, useful in .d.ts files and when tsconfig limits `types`.

options.text: It tells the compiler to emit CommonJS for this file so that it runs correctly under Node
options.why: Output format comes from the `module` option, not from reference directives.

options.text: It marks the file as Node-only, so the bundler excludes it from browser builds automatically
options.why: Bundlers ignore these directives; they only influence which declarations TypeScript loads.

explanation: `/// <reference types="…" />` declares a dependency on a types package, much like listing it in `compilerOptions.types`. It is mostly used inside `.d.ts` files that rely on another package's globals, and in a file that needs a types package the tsconfig did not include. `/// <reference path="…" />` is the file-path variant.

options.text: Type-only imports are not allowed in declaration files; move the `Foo` import into each file that uses it
options.why: Imports are allowed in .d.ts files. The problem is what the import does to the file's scope.

options.text: The interface needs `export` now, so change it to `export interface Window` so that the merge happens
options.why: Exporting it creates a module-local interface named Window; it still would not merge with the global one.

options.text: The import made the file a module, so `Window` is now module-local; wrap it in `declare global { … }`
options.why: Inside declare global the interface merges with the built-in Window again, and the import keeps working.

options.text: The DOM lib is no longer loaded once any declaration file imports a module, so add "dom" to `lib` again
options.why: The DOM lib is still loaded; TS2339 says Window exists but lacks the property.

explanation: Any top-level import or export turns a file into a module, and declarations in a module are scoped to it. The `interface Window` above therefore declares a new, unrelated local type instead of merging with the global `Window`. The fix keeps the import and moves the augmentation into `declare global { interface Window { … } }`, which is only legal inside a module.

options.text: Rename the file from `env.d.ts` to `env.ts` so that the compiler treats it as a source module
options.why: File extension does not decide module status; a .ts file with no import or export is still a script.

options.text: Add `export {};` to the file, which makes it a module so that `declare global` is allowed
options.why: Alternatively drop the declare global wrapper, since a script's interface is already global.

options.text: Replace `declare global` with `declare namespace globalThis` so that the members attach to the window object
options.why: That form is not a supported way to augment Window and would not fix the merge.

options.text: Enable `isolatedModules`, which forces every file to be treated as a module by the compiler
options.why: isolatedModules adds restrictions for single-file transpilers; it does not legalise declare global in scripts.

explanation: `declare global` means "reach out of this module into the global scope", so it only makes sense in a module. In a script file every top-level declaration is already global, so either write `interface Window { … }` without the wrapper or add `export {}` and keep the wrapper. Teams usually prefer `export {}` + `declare global` because it keeps working if an import is added later.

options.text: tsc reports TS2339, because the wildcard declaration reads the class names from the CSS file
options.why: Ambient declarations never read the CSS. They only say what shape any matching module has.

options.text: It compiles, typed as `string`, and renders `undefined` at runtime, because any key is allowed
options.why: The index signature accepts every property name, so typos are invisible to the checker.

options.text: It compiles, but `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is ignored here, so the type is `string | undefined` either way
options.why: Without that flag the type is plain string; with it, it would be string | undefined. It is never an error.

options.text: The bundler fails the build because the class does not exist in `Button.module.css`
options.why: Most bundlers just return undefined for unknown keys; nothing fails at build time.

explanation: A wildcard module declaration gives every matching file the same loose type. That makes imports compile but provides no safety for class names. To catch typos, generate a per-file declaration (for example with typed-css-modules or a TypeScript plugin that writes `Button.module.css.d.ts`), or enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` so at least the `undefined` case shows up in types.

stem: Which of these pairs of same-named declarations merge legally in one module? (Choose three.)

options.text: `export function greet() {}` followed by `export namespace greet { export const suffix = "!"; }`
options.why: A namespace after a function adds static members to it, as in greet.suffix.

options.text: `export class Point {}` followed by `export namespace Point { export const origin = new Point(); }`
options.why: Class plus namespace is the classic way to add statics such as Point.origin.

options.text: `export enum Color { Red }` and `export namespace Color { export function parse(s: string) { return Color.Red; } }`
options.why: Enums can merge with namespaces to gain helper functions such as Color.parse.

options.text: `class A { x = 1 }` and `class A { y = 2 }`
options.why: Classes never merge with each other; this is TS2300, duplicate identifier.

options.text: `export namespace greet { … }` written before `export function greet() {}`
options.why: A namespace that merges with a function or class must come after it (TS2434).

options.text: `interface Box { size: number }` and `interface Box { size: string }`
options.why: Interfaces merge, but a non-method member must have the same type in each (TS2717).

explanation: Namespaces can merge with functions, classes and enums to add static members, and many older libraries are typed this way (`jQuery` as a function with properties). The namespace must follow the function or class it extends. Classes cannot merge with classes, and same-named non-function interface members must agree on their type.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Declaration Merging (Merging namespaces with classes, functions, and enums)

stem: Under `strict`, importing a plain JavaScript package that has no typings produces the error "Could not find a declaration file for module …". Type the numeric TypeScript error code (digits only).
explanation: TS7016 is a noImplicitAny error: the module resolved to a JavaScript file, so its type would be an implicit `any`. With `noImplicitAny` off the import silently becomes `any` instead. Fix it with @types, the package's own types, or a `declare module` declaration.

stem:
With `"module": "commonjs"`, what does tsc emit for this line?

```ts
import fs = require("fs");
```

options.text: `import fs from "fs";`
options.why: CommonJS output never contains ES import statements.

options.text: `const fs = __importDefault(require("fs"));`
options.why: The interop helper is used for default imports, not for import-equals, which keeps exact CommonJS semantics.

options.text: `const fs = require("fs");`
options.why: import x = require() is TypeScript's CommonJS-native form and maps one to one onto require.

options.text: Nothing, because import-equals declarations are type-only and erased
options.why: It is erased only when fs is used purely as a type; here it stays as a value import.

explanation: `import x = require("m")` binds `x` to exactly what `module.exports` is, with no interop wrapping. It is the right way to consume an `export =` module in CommonJS code and is allowed only when emitting CommonJS (or under `module: nodenext` in .cts files). It is erased if the binding is never used as a value.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Modules (export = and import = require())

stem: In `main.ts` you want the type of the `config` object exported by `./config.ts`, without importing anything at runtime and without a top-level import. Which line works?

options.text: `type Config = typeof require("./config").config;`
options.why: require is not a type query; typeof on a call expression is not allowed in a type position.

options.text: `type Config = import("./config").config;`
options.why: config is a value, so it must be wrapped in typeof; this form only works for exported types.

options.text: `type Config = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof import>>["config"];`
options.why: `import` is not a value you can take typeof of; this does not parse.

options.text: `type Config = typeof import("./config").config;`
options.why: An import type with typeof reads a value's type, and nothing is emitted at runtime.

explanation: Import types (`import("./mod")` in a type position) refer to a module's exports inline. Use `typeof import("./config").config` for an exported value and `import("./config").Settings` for an exported type. They are erased, so they are handy in JSDoc, in global declaration files that must stay scripts, and to avoid circular runtime imports.

stem: Match each package.json field with its role in how TypeScript finds a library's typings.

options.text: Entry declaration file used when the package has no "exports" map
options.why: "types"

options.text: Per-entry-point conditions, read under node16/nodenext/bundler resolution
options.why: "exports"

options.text: Redirects declaration lookups for consumers on a matching TypeScript version range
options.why: "typesVersions"

options.text: Runtime entry point; TypeScript also looks for a .d.ts beside it
options.why: "main"

explanation: Modern resolution modes read `exports` and its `types` condition; when `exports` exists, the top-level `types` field is ignored for those consumers. Older node10-style resolution reads `types` (or `typings`), then a `.d.ts` beside `main`. `typesVersions` lets one package ship different declarations to different TypeScript versions.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Publishing (Including declarations in your npm package)

stem:
A Node project uses `"module": "nodenext"`, `"resolveJsonModule": true` and `"type": "module"` in package.json. This line fails with TS1543. What is the fix?

```ts
import data from "./data.json";
```

options.text: Switch to `import * as data from "./data.json"`, which TypeScript treats as a plain object import
options.why: Changing the import form does not help; Node still needs the JSON import attribute.

options.text: Turn off `resolveJsonModule`, which conflicts with ES modules under nodenext resolution
options.why: Without resolveJsonModule the JSON file cannot be imported at all.

options.text: Add an import attribute: `import data from "./data.json" with { type: "json" };`
options.why: Node requires `type: "json"` for JSON in ESM, and TypeScript enforces it under nodenext.

options.text: Rename the file to `data.json.ts` so that the compiler emits a JavaScript module for it
options.why: Renaming creates a TypeScript file; it no longer is JSON and needs a real export statement.

explanation: In Node's ES module loader, JSON must be imported with the `type: "json"` attribute, and since TypeScript 5.7 the compiler checks this under `module: nodenext` (TS1543). With the attribute, the default import is typed from the JSON contents, so `data.port` is a number. CommonJS files (.cts) can still import JSON without attributes.
reference: TypeScript 5.7 release notes: Validated JSON imports in --module nodenext

stem: In a module file, `declare module "core" { export function added(): void; }` (augmenting an installed, typed package `core`) is a compile error, because module augmentations may only extend declarations that already exist.

options.text: True
options.why: Current TypeScript accepts new exported declarations inside an augmentation; they type-check when imported.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: it compiles, but the augmentation only adds types, so `added` will not exist at runtime unless something patches it in.

explanation: Older docs warn that augmentations can only patch existing declarations. In practice tsc 6 accepts new exported members inside `declare module "core" { … }`, and importing `added` type-checks. The real danger is that augmentations are types only: unless some code actually adds `added` to the module at runtime, calling it throws. Prefer augmenting interfaces that the library already exposes for extension.

options.text: `clone(a: Dog): Dog`
options.why: From the last declaration, first in its block.

options.text: `clone(a: Cat): Cat`
options.why: From the last declaration, second in its block.

options.text: `clone(a: Sheep): Sheep`
options.why: From the middle declaration.

options.text: `clone(a: Animal): Animal`
options.why: From the first declaration, so it ends up last.

explanation: When interfaces merge, each later declaration's overloads are placed before the earlier ones, while the order inside each declaration is kept. So the last block (Dog, Cat) comes first, then Sheep, then Animal. This is why an augmentation can add a more specific overload that wins over a library's general one. One exception: overloads whose parameter is a single string literal type bubble to the top.

stem: With `isolatedModules` enabled, `index.ts` contains `export { User } from "./types";`, where `User` is an interface. tsc reports TS1205. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: A per-file transpiler can't tell `User` is a type and would emit a broken re-export; write `export type { User }`
options.why: Marking it type-only lets single-file tools erase the re-export safely.

options.text: Interfaces can never be re-exported from a barrel file; move consumers to import from `./types` directly
options.why: Types can be re-exported; they just need to be marked type-only under isolatedModules.

options.text: The barrel must use `export * from "./types"`, since named re-exports require the target to be a value
options.why: export * would avoid the error, but the precise fix is a type-only re-export.

options.text: isolatedModules requires every interface to be declared in a `.d.ts` file rather than in a `.ts` module
options.why: isolatedModules has no such rule; interfaces in .ts files are fine.

explanation: Tools such as esbuild, SWC and Babel compile one file at a time and can't look into `./types` to learn that `User` is only a type. If they kept `export { User } from "./types"`, the runtime would look for an export that doesn't exist. `export type { User } from "./types"` (or `export { type User }`) tells every tool it is safe to erase. The same error appears under `verbatimModuleSyntax`.

stem: After upgrading to TypeScript 6.0, a project whose tsconfig has no `types` option reports "Cannot find name 'describe'" in every test file, even though `@types/jest` is installed. Which two changes fix it? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add `"types": ["jest", "node"]` (or whichever global packages you use) to compilerOptions
options.why: TypeScript 6 defaults `types` to an empty list, so global @types packages must be listed.

options.text: Add `/// <reference types="jest" />` to the test files or to a shared test setup `.d.ts`
options.why: A reference directive pulls the package's globals into the compilation explicitly.

options.text: Reinstall `@types/jest`, because the upgrade removed it from `node_modules/@types`
options.why: The package is still installed; it is simply no longer loaded automatically.

options.text: Add `import "jest";` at the top of every test file so that the globals are registered
options.why: jest itself is not a module that declares these globals; the types live in @types/jest.

options.text: Set `"typeRoots": []`, which tells the compiler to scan every `node_modules/@types` folder again
options.why: An empty typeRoots disables lookups rather than enabling them.

explanation: Before 6.0, every package under `node_modules/@types` was added to the program automatically, which also slowed builds and leaked unrelated globals. TypeScript 6.0 changes the default of `types` to `[]`, so global-only packages such as `@types/jest` or `@types/node` must be listed or referenced. `"types": ["*"]` restores the old behaviour. Module imports such as `import express from "express"` still find `@types/express` on their own.
reference: TypeScript 6.0 release notes: types defaults to []

options.text: The `types` field must point to a `.d.mts` file whenever the package also ships an `.mjs` entry
options.why: The extension isn't what is wrong; the field is not consulted at all here.

options.text: bundler resolution never reads type declarations from `node_modules`, only from local source files
options.why: bundler resolution reads package declarations through "exports" like node16 does.

options.text: With "exports" present, top-level "types" is ignored; add a "types" condition
options.why: Resolution follows `import` to `index.mjs`, finds no `index.d.mts` beside it and reports an untyped module.

options.text: Conditional exports always require `"type": "module"` in package.json before TypeScript reads them
options.why: "type" changes how .js files are interpreted; it is not required for exports conditions.

explanation: Under node16, nodenext and bundler resolution, `exports` is the source of truth and top-level `types`/`main` are ignored for paths it covers. TypeScript resolved `import` → `./dist/index.mjs`, looked for `./dist/index.d.mts`, found none and fell back to treating the package as untyped. Fix it with `".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "import": …, "require": … }` or nested per-condition types, and check the result with arethetypeswrong.

options.text: All three lines, because everything inside `declare global` is a property of `globalThis`
options.why: Only var declarations become properties of the global object; let and const do not.

options.text: Lines 1 and 3; line 2 fails, because a global `let` is not a property of `globalThis`
options.why: This mirrors JavaScript, where top-level let bindings live outside the global object.

options.text: Only line 1, because `let` is not allowed inside `declare global` at all
options.why: let is allowed there and declares a global binding you can use by name.

options.text: Only line 3, since `globalThis` property access needs an explicit `interface GlobalThis` merge
options.why: There is no GlobalThis interface to merge; var declarations are added to typeof globalThis automatically.

explanation: TypeScript models the JavaScript rule that top-level `var` creates a property on the global object, while `let`/`const` create bindings in the global lexical scope. So `declare global { var X }` makes both `X` and `globalThis.X` valid, but a `let` is only usable by name (TS2339 on `globalThis.__BUILD__`). Use `var` for values injected onto `window`/`globalThis`.
reference: TypeScript 3.4 release notes: Type-checking for globalThis

stem: A library's typings end with `export as namespace MathLib;`. A plain script file can call `MathLib.add(1, 2)`, but the same line in a file that has an import fails with TS2686. What is the usual fix in that module?

options.text: Add `declare const MathLib: typeof import("mathlib");` to the file to recreate the global
options.why: That redeclares the global by hand and hides the real issue: the module should import the library.

options.text: Add `/// <reference types="mathlib" />` so that the UMD global becomes visible inside modules too
options.why: The reference is not the problem; modules are deliberately barred from UMD globals.

options.text: Import it: `import * as MathLib from "mathlib";`
options.why: Inside a module you are expected to use the library's module form, which also keeps the dependency explicit.

options.text: Rename the call to `window.MathLib.add` so that the access goes through the DOM lib types
options.why: Window has no MathLib member; this just changes the error to TS2339.

explanation: `export as namespace X` describes a UMD library that is both a module and, when loaded by a script tag, a global named `X`. TypeScript lets scripts use the global but reports TS2686 in modules, because a module should import its dependencies. If the global really is provided at runtime, the `allowUmdGlobalAccess` compiler option turns the check off.

options.text: `undefined`, because the subclass field definition runs after the base constructor and resets it
options.why: That is what a plain `name: …` redeclaration would do; `declare` prevents any emit.

options.text: `"a"`, because the declared literal type becomes the property's initial value at runtime
options.why: Types never create runtime values; declare only narrows the property's type.

options.text: It is a compile error, because a class cannot `declare` a property it inherits from a base
options.why: Redeclaring an inherited property with declare and a compatible type is exactly what declare fields are for.

options.text: `"base"`: `declare` only narrows the type and emits no field, so the base value survives
options.why: Without declare, the subclass would emit `name;`, which redefines the property as undefined.

explanation: Under ES2022 class-field semantics a field written in a subclass, even without an initializer, is emitted (`name;`) and redefines the property on the instance after `super()` returns, overwriting the base class value with `undefined`. `declare name: …` is purely a type annotation: tsc emits nothing for it. Use it to narrow inherited properties or to type properties a base class or framework assigns.
reference: TypeScript 3.7 release notes: useDefineForClassFields and the declare property modifier

options.text: Both import lines are removed, since each one only brings in a type
options.why: Under verbatimModuleSyntax, only an import with `type` on the whole statement is dropped.

options.text: `a.js` has no import; `b.js` keeps `import {} from "./types";`, so `./types` still runs
options.why: An inline `type` modifier erases only that specifier, and the statement remains.

options.text: Both files keep `import { User } from "./types";`, and the import fails at runtime
options.why: Type-marked specifiers are always erased; User never appears in the output.

options.text: `b.ts` is a compile error, because inline `type` modifiers aren't allowed with verbatimModuleSyntax
options.why: Inline type modifiers are allowed; they are one of the two forms the option expects.

explanation: `verbatimModuleSyntax` makes emit predictable: anything without a `type` modifier is kept as written, and anything with one is dropped. `import type { … }` disappears entirely. `import { type User }` drops the specifier but keeps the statement as `import {} from "./types"`, so the module and its side effects still load. Choose the form deliberately when side effects matter.

stem: With `verbatimModuleSyntax` on, `import { User } from "./types";`, where `User` is an interface, produces "'User' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import". Type the numeric error code (digits only).
explanation: TS1484 asks you to mark type-only imports (`import type { User }` or `import { type User }`), because under verbatimModuleSyntax the compiler will not guess which specifiers to drop. The matching re-export error is TS1205.

options.text: `import { slugify, other } from "legacy"` now fails with TS2305, because `other` isn't declared
options.why: A full ambient module declaration lists every export, so anything missing is an error.

options.text: If the file also had a top-level import, the block would become an augmentation and fail with TS2665
options.why: An untyped JavaScript module cannot be augmented; it needs an ambient declaration in a script.

options.text: The declaration also adds a runtime shim, so `slugify` works even if the package isn't installed
options.why: Declarations are erased; the package must still exist at runtime.

options.text: The block is ignored if `@types/legacy` does not exist, since ambient modules only extend @types
options.why: An ambient module declaration stands on its own; it is the typing when no other exists.

options.text: Every export is still typed `any`, exactly as with the shorthand `declare module "legacy";`
options.why: Only the bodiless shorthand gives any. This body declares precise types.

explanation: In a script file, `declare module "legacy" { … }` is an ambient module declaration that fully describes the module, so undeclared names are errors (TS2305) and declared ones get real types. In a module file, the same syntax is an augmentation, which needs an already-typed module. For an untyped JS module tsc reports TS2665. Keep such shims in import-free `.d.ts` files.

stem: A package has no "exports" field. For `import { v } from "lib"`, put the places TypeScript checks for declarations in order, from first tried to last.

options.text: The file named by `"types"` (or `"typings"`) in `node_modules/lib/package.json`
options.why: An explicit types field wins inside the package.

options.text: A `.d.ts` file next to the `"main"` entry, for example `lib/main.d.ts`
options.why: Next, TypeScript swaps the main entry's extension for .d.ts.

options.text: `node_modules/lib/index.d.ts` at the package root
options.why: The default index file is tried after main.

options.text: `node_modules/@types/lib`
options.why: DefinitelyTyped is the fallback when the package has no declarations of its own.

explanation: Without "exports", TypeScript first honours the package's declared typings, then mirrors Node's entry lookup (main, then index) with .d.ts extensions, and only then looks in `@types`. This is why stale `@types/x` packages are harmless but useless once `x` ships its own types, and why a `.d.ts` beside `main` is enough for simple packages.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Module Resolution (How TypeScript resolves modules)

stem: `types/window.d.ts` declares `interface Window { analytics: … }`. The editor is happy, but `tsc -p .` reports TS2339 for `window.analytics` in `src/main.ts`. The tsconfig has `"include": ["src"]`. What is going on?

options.text: tsc ignores `.d.ts` files unless they are listed in `"typeRoots"`, which the editor does not require
options.why: typeRoots is only for packages of global types; loose .d.ts files just need to be in the program.

options.text: `types/` is outside `include`, so tsc never loads that file; add it to `include`
options.why: An editor can pick it up when the file is open; the CLI only loads files the tsconfig includes.

options.text: Window augmentations only take effect when the declaration file has the `.global.d.ts` suffix
options.why: There is no such suffix convention; any included script-style .d.ts works.

options.text: The DOM lib overrides user-declared Window members during a full build, but not in the editor
options.why: lib types merge with your declarations in both environments.

explanation: Declaration files only count if they are in the program: matched by `include`/`files`, referenced with `/// <reference path>`, or pulled in through imports. Editors sometimes load an open file into an inferred project, which hides the problem until CI runs `tsc`. Use `"include": ["src", "types"]` or move the file under `src`.

stem:
A team enables `erasableSyntaxOnly` so that Node can run their `.ts` files by stripping types. Which two declarations in this file are errors (TS1294)? (Choose two.)

```ts
namespace Util { export const v = 1; }      // 1
declare namespace Ambient { const w: number; } // 2
namespace TypesOnly { export type T = string; } // 3
export enum Color { Red }                    // 4
export interface Point { x: number }         // 5
```

options.text: Line 1, a namespace that holds a runtime value
options.why: A namespace with values compiles to an IIFE, which type stripping can't produce.

options.text: Line 2, the `declare namespace`
options.why: Ambient declarations emit nothing, so they are erasable.

options.text: Line 3, a namespace that contains only types
options.why: A types-only namespace is erased completely, so it is allowed.

options.text: Line 4, the enum
options.why: Enums generate a runtime object, so they need real compilation, not just erasure.

options.text: Line 5, the interface
options.why: Interfaces are pure types and are always erasable.

explanation: Node's built-in TypeScript support (and similar tools) works by deleting type syntax, not by compiling. `erasableSyntaxOnly` (TypeScript 5.8) flags constructs that need code generation: enums, namespaces with runtime content, parameter properties and `import x = require()`. Ambient and type-only namespaces remain fine because they vanish entirely.

stem: Match each import with what tsc emits for it. The first three lines are compiled to CommonJS (esModuleInterop on, and each binding used as a value); the last is compiled to ES modules with `verbatimModuleSyntax`.

options.text: Nothing at all
options.why: erased

options.text: `const greet = require("greet");`
options.why: plain require

options.text: `const greet_1 = __importDefault(require("greet"));`
options.why: interop helper

options.text: `import {} from "greet";`
options.why: side-effect import kept

explanation: Type-only statements vanish. import-equals maps directly onto `require`. A default import of a CommonJS module goes through `__importDefault`, which wraps `module.exports` as `{ default: module.exports }` unless the module is marked `__esModule`. Under verbatimModuleSyntax, an inline `type` specifier is dropped but the statement stays as an empty import.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Modules Reference (Module format interop)

options.text: A shim file cannot redeclare a package that has types, so tsc drops the package typings with a warning
options.why: There is no warning and nothing is dropped from the package; the ambient module simply wins resolution.

options.text: Ambient modules only merge with `@types` packages, not with typings bundled inside the package itself
options.why: Where the typings live is not the point; whether the shim file is a script or a module is.

options.text: In a script, this is an ambient module declaration that replaces "core"'s typings; add `export {}` to make it an augmentation
options.why: As an augmentation inside a module file, the block merges with the package's real declarations instead.

options.text: The augmentation needs `export declare function other()` with `declare` repeated inside the block
options.why: Members of an ambient context are implicitly declared; adding declare changes nothing.

explanation: The same `declare module "core" { … }` syntax means two different things. In a script file it is an ambient module declaration, which TypeScript uses as the module's complete typing instead of resolving the package, so `run` disappears. In a module file (any top-level import or `export {}`) it is a module augmentation that merges into the resolved package typings. Shim files that patch existing packages must therefore be modules.

stem: A CommonJS library does `module.exports = function greet(name) { … }`, but its hand-written typings say `export default greet;`. An ESM consumer (`"type": "module"`, `module: nodenext`) writes `import greet from "greet"; greet("a");`. What happens?

options.text: It type-checks and runs, because Node's default import of a CommonJS module is `module.exports`
options.why: At runtime that is true, but TypeScript believes the typings, which describe a `default` property.

options.text: It type-checks, but crashes at runtime, because Node gives ESM consumers `module.exports.default`
options.why: Node gives the default import module.exports itself, so the call would work; the error is at compile time.

options.text: It fails with TS1479, because an ES module may never import a CommonJS package under nodenext
options.why: ESM importing CommonJS is allowed; the problem is the mismatched typings.

options.text: TS2349: the default import is typed as the module object; `.default()` compiles but crashes
options.why: The typings should say `export = greet;` to match what module.exports actually is.

explanation: In a CommonJS declaration file, `export default x` means "module.exports.default is x". An ESM default import of a CJS module receives `module.exports` itself, so TypeScript types `greet` as the whole module object (with a `.default` property) and calling it is TS2349. The workaround `greet.default("a")` type-checks but calls undefined at runtime. Correct typings for `module.exports = fn` use `export = greet;`. Tools like arethetypeswrong flag this "incorrect default export".
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Modules Reference (export = and ESM interop)

stem: An older codebase has `"esModuleInterop": false` and code like `import * as greet from "greet"; greet("a");`, where greet's typings use `export = greet` for a function. After upgrading to TypeScript 6.0, what happens and what is the right migration?

options.text: Nothing changes; esModuleInterop false keeps working in 6.0 and only `module: amd` users see new errors
options.why: In 6.0, esModuleInterop false is deprecated and reported as TS5107.

options.text: TS5107 deprecates the false setting; with interop on, `greet()` gives TS2497, so switch to `import greet from "greet"`
options.why: Under interop a namespace import is an object and can't be called; use a default import.

options.text: TS 6.0 removes `import * as` syntax for CommonJS modules entirely, so every such line must use require
options.why: Namespace imports are still valid; they just can't be called when they wrap a function export.

options.text: Set `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"` permanently, since TypeScript 7 will restore the old interop default
options.why: The flag only delays the error; TypeScript 7 drops the setting altogether.

explanation: TypeScript 6.0 deprecates `esModuleInterop: false` and `allowSyntheticDefaultImports: false` (TS5107, silenceable with `ignoreDeprecations: "6.0"` until 7.0). With interop on, a namespace import follows the ES rule that it is a plain object, so calling it is TS2497. Migrate calls on `import * as x` of callable `export =` modules to `import x from "m"`. tsc then emits `__importDefault(require("m"))`, which works for both real ES modules and plain CommonJS.

stem: `web` re-exports `Request` from `core` (`export { Request } from "core"`). Which three statements about module augmentation are true in TypeScript 6? (Choose three.)

options.text: `declare module "web" { interface Request { user?: string } }` in a module file adds `user` to the Request type that `web` re-exports
options.why: tsc 6 resolves the re-export to the original interface and merges the augmentation into it.

options.text: Augmenting a specifier that does not resolve, such as `declare module "not-installed" { … }` in a module file, is error TS2664
options.why: An augmentation must target a module the compiler can resolve.

options.text: An augmentation that adds `export const flag: boolean` type-checks on import, but nothing creates `flag` at runtime
options.why: Augmentations are type-only; they never change the module's real exports.

options.text: An augmentation applies only to the file that contains it, so each file using `req.user` must repeat it
options.why: Once part of the program, an augmentation affects every file that sees that module.

options.text: Augmentations work only for packages under `node_modules/@types`, not for packages that bundle their own `.d.ts`
options.why: Bundled typings can be augmented just the same, as long as the target resolves.

explanation: An augmentation patches the program-wide view of a module. It must target a resolvable module (TS2664 otherwise, or TS2665 for an untyped JS module). When the target re-exports an interface, current TypeScript merges into the original declaration, although augmenting the declaring module (`core`, or `express-serve-static-core` for Express) is still the clearest choice. Everything added is compile-time only.

options.text: `index.d.ts`, because `typesVersions` is consulted only when `types` is missing
options.why: typesVersions applies on top of types: when the version range matches, lookups are redirected.

options.text: `index.d.ts`, because the `>=5.0` range does not match 6.0 under npm semver rules
options.why: 6.0 is greater than 5.0, so the range matches.

options.text: `ts5/index.d.ts`, because tsc 6 matches the `>=5.0` range and the `*` pattern remaps the lookup into `ts5/`
options.why: Consumers on TypeScript below 5.0 would still get the root index.d.ts.

options.text: Both files, merged together, with `ts5/index.d.ts` taking precedence on conflicts
options.why: Exactly one file is chosen; declarations from different typesVersions folders never merge.

explanation: `typesVersions` lets a package ship newer declarations (using newer type features) to newer compilers while older ones keep the root files. TypeScript picks the first range that matches its own version and rewrites the requested path through the mapping, so `index.d.ts` becomes `ts5/index.d.ts`.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Publishing (Version selection with typesVersions)

stem: A dual package has `"type": "module"`, `index.js` (ESM) and `index.cjs` (CommonJS). Which "exports" map gives both ESM and CommonJS consumers declarations in the right module format?

options.text: `{ ".": { "types": "./index.d.ts", "import": "./index.js", "require": "./index.cjs" } }`
options.why: One .d.ts in a type:module package is read as ESM types even for require consumers, which arethetypeswrong flags as "Masquerading as ESM".

options.text: `{ ".": { "import": "./index.js", "require": "./index.cjs" } }` plus a top-level `"types": "./index.d.ts"`
options.why: With exports present, modern resolution ignores the top-level types field.

options.text: `{ ".": { "import": { "types": "./index.d.ts", "default": "./index.js" }, "require": { "types": "./index.d.cts", "default": "./index.cjs" } } }`
options.why: Each condition gets declarations whose extension matches the format of its JavaScript.

options.text: `{ ".": { "default": "./index.js", "types": "./index.d.ts" } }`, letting Node pick CommonJS automatically
options.why: default comes first and matches everything, so there is no CommonJS entry and types is never reached.

explanation: A declaration file's format follows the same rules as JavaScript: `.d.ts` in a `"type": "module"` package describes ESM, `.d.cts` describes CommonJS. A single shared `.d.ts` tells CommonJS consumers they are importing ESM, which hides real differences in default exports and interop. Nesting `types` inside each condition (and keeping `types` first within each) gives every consumer accurate declarations; verify with `npx @arethetypeswrong/cli`.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Modules Reference (package.json "exports" and file extensions)

stem: With `module: commonjs` and esModuleInterop, `import greet from "greet";` compiles to `const greet_1 = ____(require("greet"));`. Type the name of the helper function in the blank.
explanation: `__importDefault(mod)` returns `mod` if it has `__esModule` set (a transpiled ES module) and otherwise wraps it as `{ default: mod }`, so a default import of a plain CommonJS module gets `module.exports`. Its sibling `__importStar` handles `import * as x`. With `importHelpers`, they come from `tslib` instead of being inlined.

stem: After adding a dependency, the build fails inside `node_modules` with TS2403: "Subsequent variable declarations must have the same type. Variable 'appName' must be of type 'string', but here has type 'number'." Two installed packages each `declare var appName` globally. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Deduplicating so that only one copy or version of the conflicting typings is installed fixes the root cause
options.why: Duplicate or mismatched global typings, often two versions of one @types package, are the usual source.

options.text: `skipLibCheck: true` makes the build pass, but `appName` keeps the first declaration's type, which may be wrong
options.why: It skips reporting errors inside .d.ts files instead of resolving the conflict.

options.text: Wrapping your own code in `declare global { … }` scopes the variable and resolves the clash
options.why: The conflict is between two library declaration files; your code can't rescope them.

options.text: Changing one declaration to `let appName` fixes it, because `let` and `var` globals can coexist
options.why: Redeclaring a block-scoped global alongside a var is still an error.

options.text: Setting `"types": []` always removes both packages, including any that your source imports directly
options.why: `types` only controls automatic global inclusion; packages that your code imports are still loaded.

explanation: Global declarations from all files share one scope, so two `declare var appName` with different types collide. The real fix is to remove the duplicate, for example with `npm dedupe` or package-manager overrides that pin one version of the @types package. `skipLibCheck` is a common pragmatic choice that speeds builds, but it hides such conflicts rather than fixing them.

stem: A library wants a private brand key that no other symbol can impersonate. Which declaration is valid?

options.text: `let brand: unique symbol = Symbol("brand");`, since `unique symbol` may annotate any variable
options.why: A unique symbol must be const or a readonly static property; this is TS1332.

options.text: `type Brand = unique symbol;` exported from the `.d.ts` and reused across packages
options.why: A type alias to unique symbol is TS1335; each unique symbol type belongs to one declaration.

options.text: `declare const brand: unique symbol;` in the `.d.ts`, then `interface Token { [brand]: true }`
options.why: Each unique symbol declaration gets its own type, so only this exact symbol can key the property.

options.text: `const brand = Symbol.for("brand") as unique symbol;`, since `Symbol.for` returns a registry symbol
options.why: Asserting to unique symbol is TS1335, and anyone can recreate a registry symbol with Symbol.for.

explanation: `unique symbol` is a subtype of `symbol` tied to one specific declaration. Writing `declare const brand: unique symbol` in a declaration file creates a symbol type that nothing else can match, which is ideal for nominal brands and private-ish keys in public typings. It is only allowed on `const` declarations and `readonly static` properties (otherwise TS1332, or TS1335 in places such as type aliases and assertions).

options.text: `r1: "first"`, `r2: "general"`, because overloads are checked in the order they appear in the source
options.why: Merged interfaces put later declarations' overloads first, so source order is not preserved.

options.text: `r1: "second"`, `r2: "literal"`, because later blocks' overloads come first
options.why: The later f wins, and the g that takes a single string literal is moved to the top anyway.

options.text: `r1: "first" | "second"`, `r2: "general" | "literal"`, because merged overloads become unions
options.why: Overload resolution picks one signature; it never unions return types.

options.text: A compile error, because two `f` signatures with identical parameter lists conflict when merged
options.why: Methods can be overloaded across merged declarations; only non-method properties must agree.

explanation: Merged interface overloads are ordered with later declarations first, so the second `f` is tried before the first and wins for `"s"`. For `g`, ordering alone would put the `"lit"` overload first as well, and there is also a specific rule: signatures whose parameter is a single string literal type are bubbled to the top of the merged list. Library authors rely on this when an augmentation must override a general signature.
